summary: Specifies a new type for the 6LoWPAN routing header carrying a packet's deadline time, to support forwarding and scheduling decisions for time-critical machine-to-machine applications in time-synchronized constrained networks.

eli5.summary: Each packet carries a time stamp saying it must arrive by then, so devices can prioritize the most urgent ones.

questions: time critical packets in constrained networks
what is the 6lowpan routing header deadline time
how do 6lowpan packets carry a deadline
what does the d flag do in deadline-6lorhe
subtitle: A small header that tells every router on a low-power wireless network when a packet must arrive, so late packets can be dropped.

tldr.problem: Time-critical machine-to-machine traffic on low-power, lossy networks must reach its receiver within strict time bounds, but routers have no way to see how urgent a packet is.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9034 defines Deadline-6LoRHE, a new elective 6LoWPAN routing header type that carries the packet deadline time (DT) and, optionally, an origination time delta (OTD), in a compressed form that nodes in a time-synchronized network can compare with their own clock.
tldr.outcome: Nodes can drop a packet whose deadline has passed (when the D flag is set) and the delay a packet suffered can be measured, but the scheme only works where time is synchronized and the network is a controlled environment.

today: RFC 9034 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC, so it remains the definition of Deadline-6LoRHE.

sections.title: Why Packets Need a Deadline
sections.content:
Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) are likely to be deployed for real-time industrial applications that need end-to-end delay guarantees. A Deterministic Network ("DetNet") typically requires some data packets to reach their receivers within strict time bounds, and intermediate nodes can use deadline information to make forwarding and scheduling decisions.

RFC 9034 builds on RFC 8138, which defines the 6LoWPAN Routing Header (6LoRH). It adds a new type of the Elective 6LoWPAN Routing Header (6LoRHE), called Deadline-6LoRHE, that holds the deadline time: the time of latest acceptable delivery.

Time-synchronization techniques themselves are out of scope. The text names IEEE 1588, IEEE 802.1AS and IEEE 802.15.4-2015 Time-Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH) as examples. A 6TiSCH network is used to describe the design, but the header can be used in any time-synchronized 6LoWPAN network, and Bluetooth Low Energy mesh and Wi-SUN are mentioned as other cases of interest.
sections.eli5: Some messages in factories are like a train that must leave on time. This document lets a message carry its own "be there by" time so helpers on the way know how urgent it is.

sections.title: Deadline Time and Moving Between Clocks
sections.content:
The Deadline Time (DT) is the time by which the application expects the packet to reach the receiver. It is the packet origination time plus the maximum delay the application allows. The header can also carry the Origination Time Delta (OTD), which is the time the packet was enqueued, written as a value to be subtracted from DT. That gives a close estimate of the total delay the packet has suffered.

Times are counted in units set by a scaling field in the header. In a time-slotted network such as 6TiSCH, the Network ASN (Absolute Slot Number) can be the time unit.

When a packet crosses into a network that uses a different reference clock, the DT is rewritten to the same deadline expressed in the new network's clock. The packet is made to look as if it had originated current_dly time units earlier, so the origination time in the new network is the current time there minus the delay already used. The RFC's worked example has three networks in different time zones, where a packet that arrives at time 5000 in the third network is treated as originated at 4550 because 450 was already spent.

The various kinds of delay (queuing, MAC-layer contention, serialization, propagation, processing) are not told apart when deciding whether the deadline has passed.
sections.eli5: If a letter crosses into a country with a different clock, the post office rewrites the deadline in local time. It also remembers how much time was already used up, so the letter is not given a fresh start.

sections.title: The Deadline-6LoRHE Format
sections.content:
The header starts with the generic 6LoRHE layout from RFC 8138: the bits 101, a 5-bit Length, and a type byte. For Deadline-6LoRHE the 6LoRH Type is 7. Then come these fixed fields:

  • D flag (1 bit): set by the sender. If 1, a 6LoWPAN Router (6LR) MUST drop the packet when the deadline has elapsed. If 0, the packet MAY be forwarded on an exception basis, but only if the node is not short of resources and there is reason to think downstream nodes would find it useful (for delay measurements, for example).
  • TU (2 bits): the time unit for DT and OTD. 00 is seconds and fractional seconds, 10 is Network ASN, and 01 and 11 are reserved.
  • DTL (4 bits): the length of DT in hex digits, minus one.
  • OTL (3 bits): the length of OTD in hex digits. If it is 0, OTD is absent. It MUST NOT exceed DTL plus one.
  • BinaryPt (6 bits): a signed value that places the binary point in DT, in the range -32 to 31. Positive values give more bits to the integer part and so a larger range. Negative values give more bits to the fraction and so finer precision.

DT follows, and it is 4 to 64 bits long. OTD, if present, is 4 to 28 bits long and gives the origination time as a negative offset from DT. Because OTD is a delta, it needs fewer bits than DT.
sections.eli5: The header is a small form with tick boxes. One box says "throw it away if late", others say what units the clock uses and how many digits the time has.

sections.title: Compressed Time and the Safety Factor
sections.content:
To keep the header small, times are sent modulo a range. The sender works out how many bits it needs, N_bits, and sets DTL = (N_bits - 1) / 4. The range of values is Epoch_Range(DTL) = 2^(4*(DTL+1)). With DTL of 0 there are only 16 values. With DTL of 15 the 64-bit field is enough to hold an NTP 64-bit timestamp.

The integer part has N = 4*(DTL+1)/2 + BinaryPt bits. The sender must pick N so that the deadline minus the origination time is less than 2^N. Otherwise a node cannot tell a packet that is nearly expired from one that is far from its deadline.

That is not enough on its own, because the origination time is not always in the header. If a node sees a current time just after DT, it cannot tell whether the packet was just launched or the clock has wrapped around. So the RFC adds a SAFETY_FACTOR, set to 20%. The sender MUST ensure (DT_abs - OT_abs) < 2^N*(1-SAFETY_FACTOR), and every node tests whether ((CT - DT) mod 2^N) > SAFETY_FACTOR*2^N. If the test fails, the deadline has expired. All nodes MUST use the same SAFETY_FACTOR, and the packet must be tested at least once in every subinterval of that length.

The worked example uses a 6TiSCH network with 10 ms slots. The packet is originated at ASN 54400 (0xD480) with a one-second maximum delay (0x64 slots), so DT is 0xD4E4. It is encoded as DTL = 3, OTL = 2, TU = 0b10, BinaryPt = 8, DT = 0xD4E4 and OTD = 0x64. Appendix A of the RFC walks through the six orderings of OT, CT and DT to show which ones mean the deadline has passed.
sections.eli5: A clock that wraps around, like the hands of a wall clock, can be confusing about whether it is 3 o'clock today or yesterday. The safety factor leaves a gap so helpers can still tell whether a packet is early or late.

sections.title: Three Network Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC describes three scenarios in a constrained time-synchronized LLN made of subnets whose 6LoWPAN Border Routers (6LBRs) may use different reference clocks.

  • Same DODAG. The sender includes a Deadline-6LoRHE, and each 6LR forwards hop by hop to the 6LBR. In RPL non-storing mode the 6LBR sends the packet down in an IPv6-in-IPv6 tunnel. It copies the Deadline-6LoRHE to the outer header and removes it from the inner one. At the tunnel endpoint the header is copied back to the inner packet before delivery.
  • Dissimilar L2 technologies. The header is used from the sender to the 6LBR. After that the packet is encoded as the other time-synchronized network requires, which is outside this document. In-situ OAM is mentioned as one mechanism that could carry it, with the deadline updated to the new network's time.
  • Different DODAGs. This combines the first two. The first 6LBR hands the packet over a likely wired, time-synchronized backhaul, and the second 6LBR updates the Deadline-6LoRHE by adding or subtracting the time difference between the two DODAGs.

The third scenario includes a calculation. A packet generated at ASN 20000 with a one-second limit (100 slots of 10 ms) that reaches the first 6LBR at ASN 20030 has 30 ASNs left.
sections.eli5: The packet gets its deadline sticker at the start of the trip. At each border between two places that keep time differently, a border guard rewrites the sticker in the local time.

sections.title: Time Synchronization Needs
sections.content:
The deadline only means something if sender and receiver share a sense of time. The RFC does not choose a method. It mentions beaconing among nodes in a 6TiSCH network, and networks in which nodes sync to an external reference clock over NTP.

The number of hex digits in DT, and how many of its bits count whole units, set the meaning of DT equal to 0. With DTL of 0 only 4 bits count time units, so time synchronization between sender and receiver has to be tighter than 16 units. Moving the binary point so that all bits are fractional makes the requirement tighter still.

For TU of 00, DTL of 15 and BinaryPt of 0, the epoch is by default January 1, 1900 at 00:00 UTC, and the resolution is 2^-32 seconds. That format wraps around every 2^32 seconds, which is roughly 136 years. For TU of 10 with 10 ms slots and DTL of 15, the ASN would take over a year to wrap, and typically fewer hex digits are used.
sections.eli5: Everyone has to agree on what time it is. If one helper's watch is far off, they will wrongly throw away good packets or keep late ones.

sections.title: The IANA Registration
sections.content: RFC 9034 defines a new Elective 6LoWPAN Routing Header Type. IANA assigned the value 7 from the 6LoWPAN Dispatch Page 1 number space, with the description Deadline-6LoRHE, in the Elective 6LoWPAN Routing Header Type registry.
sections.eli5: The new header got its own number, 7, in the official list so nobody else uses it for something different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4944, RFC 6282 and RFC 6553 apply. The compressed format is logically equivalent to the full inline format, so it does not open a new threat compared with RFC 6550, RFC 6553 and RFC 6554.

The mechanism is designed for controlled operational environments such as industrial process control and automation. To avoid misuse of deadline information, which could lead to a Denial of Service (DoS) attack, the network needs provisioning and management of resources for flows with deadlines, performance monitoring and admission control. The security considerations of the DetNet architecture (RFC 8655) mostly apply too.

Marking flows with deadlines may tell attackers more about the data flows. Because precise time synchronization is required, its accuracy, availability and integrity are of critical importance, and RFC 7384 discusses that topic.
sections.eli5: A fake "very urgent" sticker could be used to hog the line, so the network owner has to control who may use deadlines. Keeping the clocks honest matters too.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the header in octets.

fields.name: D
fields.desc: If 1, drop the packet when the deadline has elapsed.

fields.name: TU
fields.desc: Time unit for DT and OTD.

fields.name: DTL
fields.desc: DT length in hex digits, minus one.

fields.name: OTL
fields.desc: OTD length in hex digits; 0 means absent.

fields.name: BinaryPt
fields.desc: Signed position of the binary point in DT.

items.label: Seconds
items.desc: Time in seconds and fractional seconds.

items.label: Network ASN
items.desc: Absolute Slot Number of the time-slotted network.
